content_sections.title: Build a bounded situation
content_sections.body_text: Situation: A visitor is looking for Gate 4. The departure time is 5:20. The visitor needs direct help from a friend or a staff member. Keep these two facts visible while choosing what to say; do not add facts that the situation does not give.

content_sections.title: Match wording to the person
content_sections.body_text: To a friend: ‘Help me find Gate 4, please.’ To staff: ‘Excuse me. Can you help me find Gate 4, please?’ The greeting and fuller wording suit an unfamiliar listener. Both requests name a clear action, so the helper knows what to do.

content_sections.title: Model and rehearse the exchange
content_sections.body_text: Visitor: ‘Excuse me. Can you help me find Gate 4, please?’ Staff: ‘Yes. Go straight; Gate 4 is on the left.’ Visitor: ‘Thank you.’ Rehearse both roles. Then use the shorter request with a friend and keep the response relevant to finding the gate.

content_sections.title: Mark word stress and self-check
content_sections.body_text: VIS-i-tor has three syllables; VIS carries the main stress. Make VIS clearer and slightly longer, then say the whole word at normal speed. Record one staff exchange. Check: the request fits the relationship, names Gate 4, receives useful help, and keeps stress inside VIS-i-tor rather than stressing an entire sentence.
